Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a common fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis. It primarily affects leaves, fruit, and young shoots, creating dark, scabby lesions that reduce fruit quality and overall tree vigor.
symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown velvety spots on leaves
Lesions may have a yellow halo around the scab
Infected fruit develop rough, corky, scabby patches
Severely infected leaves may turn yellow and fall prematurely
Young shoots may become distorted or stunted
management: Apply appropriate fungicides during bud break and early leaf growth stages
Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves to reduce overwintering spores
Avoid overhead irrigation that keeps foliage wet for extended periods
Prune trees to improve air circulation
prevention: Select scab-resistant apple varieties where possible
Monitor weather conditions during spring bloom for high infection risk periods
Maintain proper tree spacing to encourage air circulation
Apply preventive fungicide programs during critical risk windows
Apple___Apple_scab.severity_note: Scab can significantly reduce marketable fruit yield if left unmanaged.
Apple___Apple_scab.disclaimer: Consult a local agricultural expert or extension service for variety-specific and region-specific fungicide recommendations.

Apple___Black_rot.description: Apple black rot is a fungal disease caused by Botryosphaeria obtusa. It affects the fruit, leaves, and bark of apple trees, causing distinctive rotting of fruit and leaf lesions known as frog-eye leaf spot.
symptoms: Circular tan to brown lesions on leaves with a purple border (frog-eye leaf spot)
Dark, sunken cankers on branches and bark
Fruit develop brown rotting areas that may eventually turn entirely black and shriveled
Infected fruit may remain attached to the tree as mummified remains
Leaf lesions can cause early defoliation
management: Remove mummified fruit from trees and orchard floor
Prune out dead, diseased, or cankered wood and dispose of properly
Apply approved fungicides during the growing season as part of a spray program
Maintain general tree health through proper nutrition and irrigation
prevention: Practice good orchard sanitation by removing debris
Avoid wounding bark as wounds provide infection sites
Manage fire blight infections which can serve as entry points
Monitor trees regularly during the growing season
Apple___Black_rot.severity_note: Can cause complete loss of marketable fruit in severely infected orchards.
Apple___Black_rot.disclaimer: Consult a local agricultural extension service for region-specific management recommendations.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Corn common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. It is one of the most widespread foliar diseases of maize, producing rust-colored pustules on both leaf surfaces, which can reduce photosynthesis and yield under heavy infection.
symptoms: Small, circular to elongated brick-red to cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules break open to release rust-colored powdery spores
Heavily infected leaves may turn yellow and die prematurely
Pustules can also appear on husks and sheaths in severe cases
management: Apply appropriate foliar fungicides when rust is detected early, particularly on susceptible varieties
Monitor fields regularly starting from the vegetative stages
Ensure adequate plant spacing to reduce humidity within the canopy
prevention: Plant rust-resistant maize hybrids where available
Avoid planting in areas with a history of severe rust outbreaks without resistant varieties
Scout fields early in the season to catch infections before they spread
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.severity_note: Yield losses are generally low in resistant varieties but can be significant in susceptible ones under favorable conditions.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.disclaimer: Consult local agricultural extension services for hybrid selection and fungicide recommendations in your region.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight (NLB), caused by Exserohilum turcicum, is a significant foliar disease of maize. It produces large, cigar-shaped lesions that can coalesce and cause extensive leaf death, affecting grain fill when upper leaves are lost.
symptoms: Long, elliptical (cigar-shaped) grayish-green to tan lesions on leaves
Lesions typically 2.5 to 15 cm long
In humid conditions, dark gray-green spore masses appear on lesion surfaces
Multiple lesions can merge, causing large areas of leaf tissue to die
Lesions generally start on lower leaves and progress upward
management: Apply fungicides at the first sign of infection, particularly if the disease appears before tasseling
Incorporate crop residue after harvest to reduce inoculum
Rotate with non-host crops such as soybean or small grains
prevention: Select NLB-resistant or tolerant maize hybrids
Practice crop rotation to reduce residue-borne inoculum
Avoid dense planting which increases canopy humidity
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.severity_note: Losses are greatest when infection occurs before silking. Late-season infections have less impact on yield.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.disclaimer: Fungicide efficacy varies by product and timing. Consult local extension recommendations.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Potato early blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. Despite its name, it often affects older, stressed plants later in the season. It produces distinctive concentric ring lesions on leaves and can also affect stems and tubers.
symptoms: Dark brown to black lesions with concentric rings forming a target-like pattern
Lesions typically start on older, lower leaves
Yellow tissue (chlorosis) may surround the lesions
Severely affected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely
Dark, sunken lesions may appear on the stem and tubers
management: Apply fungicides when disease first appears and repeat as required
Remove and destroy severely infected plant material
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which can increase susceptibility
Ensure consistent irrigation to avoid plant stress
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers
Rotate potato crops with non-host crops for at least two to three years
Select early-blight-tolerant varieties
Avoid wounding plants during cultivation
Potato___Early_blight.severity_note: Can cause significant defoliation and reduce tuber yield and quality if unmanaged.
Potato___Early_blight.disclaimer: Consult local agricultural extension services for locally registered fungicide options.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Potato late blight is a destructive disease caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans. It is historically known as one of the most economically damaging crop diseases. Under favorable cool, wet conditions it can spread very rapidly and destroy an entire crop within days.
symptoms: Water-soaked, irregular pale green lesions on leaves that quickly turn brown to black
White fluffy mold (sporangia) visible on the underside of lesions in humid conditions
Stems develop dark brown, water-soaked lesions
Infected tubers develop reddish-brown to purple discoloration beneath the skin
In wet weather, the entire plant canopy can collapse very rapidly
management: Apply protective fungicides before infection and curative fungicides at first sign of disease
Remove and destroy infected plant material promptly; do not compost
Avoid overhead irrigation particularly in the evening
Harvest tubers as soon as practically possible to reduce tuber infections
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers
Use late-blight-resistant potato varieties
Monitor weather forecasts for high-risk conditions (cool temperatures, high humidity)
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for at least two years
Potato___Late_blight.severity_note: Late blight can destroy a crop extremely rapidly under favorable conditions. Early detection and immediate action are critical.
Potato___Late_blight.disclaimer: Late blight management requires prompt, expert intervention. Contact your local agricultural extension immediately upon suspected infection.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Tomato bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas species (primarily X. vesicatoria and related species). It affects leaves, stems, and fruit, causing significant cosmetic damage to fruit and defoliation under severe infection.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that enlarge to dark brown, irregular lesions
Lesions often have a yellow halo surrounding them
Spots may have a greasy or water-soaked appearance initially
Severely infected leaves may turn yellow and fall, exposing fruit to sunscald
Fruit develop small, raised, rough, brown spots that may crack
management: Apply copper-based bactericides as a protective measure, especially during wet conditions
Remove and destroy heavily infected plant material
Avoid working in the field when plants are wet to prevent further spread
Provide adequate plant spacing to improve air circulation
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Apply copper bactericides preventively during periods of wet, warm weather
Avoid overhead irrigation where possible
Rotate tomatoes with non-solanaceous crops for two or more years
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.severity_note: Can cause extensive defoliation and fruit damage, particularly in warm humid conditions.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.disclaimer: Bacterial diseases can be difficult to manage once established. Early preventive action is more effective than curative treatment.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Tomato early blight is caused by Alternaria solani. It is a common fungal disease that typically affects mature or stressed plants, producing characteristic target-spot lesions on older lower leaves and progressing upward.
symptoms: Dark brown lesions with concentric rings creating a bull's-eye or target appearance
Lesions surrounded by a yellow halo
Disease typically starts on older lower leaves and progresses upward
Affected leaves may turn yellow and drop prematurely
Dark, sunken lesions can also appear on stems and fruit near the stem end
management: Apply appropriate fungicides at the first sign of disease
Remove and dispose of infected lower leaves
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
Mulch the soil surface to reduce soil splashing of spores onto lower leaves
prevention: Use certified disease-free transplants
Practice crop rotation for two to three years with non-solanaceous crops
Stake or cage plants to keep foliage off the soil
Water at the base of plants to keep foliage dry
Tomato___Early_blight.severity_note: Severe defoliation can reduce fruit quality and yield if disease progresses unchecked.
Tomato___Early_blight.disclaimer: Consult local agricultural extension services for locally registered fungicide recommendations.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Tomato late blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans, the same oomycete pathogen responsible for potato late blight. It can destroy plants extremely rapidly under cool, moist conditions and represents one of the most serious threats to tomato crops.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked, pale green to dark brown lesions on leaves
White mold (sporangia) visible on the underside of lesions under humid conditions
Stem lesions that are brown, water-soaked, and can cause the stem to collapse
Fruit develop large, firm, brown, greasy-looking lesions
The entire plant can rapidly collapse and die in severe cases
management: Apply preventive or curative fungicides immediately upon first signs of disease
Remove and destroy infected plants; do not leave debris in the field
Avoid overhead irrigation especially in the evening
Monitor neighboring fields and surrounding area for infection sources
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant tomato varieties
Use certified disease-free transplants
Monitor weather conditions for periods of cool temperatures and high humidity
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops and avoid fields with a history of late blight
Tomato___Late_blight.severity_note: Late blight can destroy a tomato crop within days under favorable conditions. Immediate expert consultation is strongly advised.
Tomato___Late_blight.disclaimer: Late blight is a notifiable disease in some regions. Contact your local agricultural extension or plant health authority immediately upon suspected detection.
